title: A generative diffusion framework for physically consistent 3D turbulence
abstract: Synthesizing fully developed three-dimensional turbulence remains a long-standing problem in fluid mechanics and an open challenge for generative modeling. This difficulty arises from extreme dimensionality, multiscale fluctuations, strong intermittency, and the need to satisfy exact physical constraints, including incompressibility and prescribed mass and momentum fluxes under given boundary conditions. We propose a physics-constrained diffusion model in which some a priori constraints can be incorporated directly into the generative dynamics. Using rotating turbulence as a paradigmatic system with key geophysical applications, we assess the proposed framework. Here, we show that it enables stable and statistically faithful single-time synthesis of inertial-range three-dimensional turbulent velocity fields, accurately reproducing anisotropic energy spectra, intermittent statistics, and physical constraints, whereas standard denoising diffusion probabilistic models exhibit multiscale statistical deviations, violations of physical consistency, and substantially slower training convergence, thereby pointing to broader implications for generative modeling of high-dimensional, physically constrained complex systems.

title: Deep diffractive optical neural networks for detecting skyrmionic topologies of light and their live training
abstract: Optical skyrmions are topological forms of structured light offering an unbounded encoding alphabet robust to perturbations. However, their practical use is limited by the absence of a topological detector, since states distinguished by their topological invariant, N , are not necessarily orthogonal. Here, we demonstrate the first deterministic detector for optical skyrmions using a deep diffractive neural network trained in real time, with the number of training parameters reduced by a factor of 1000. The network comprises two independent processing channels, each containing five diffractive layers, that map input topologies onto spatially separated output channels, enabling identification of N . We demonstrate the detector using 81 topologies constructed from vectorial Laguerre-Gaussian modes, achieving high accuracy even at noise levels that preclude conventional Stokes polarimetry. Finally, we transmit and recover an image encoded using a 15-level topological alphabet with negligible crosstalk, demonstrating a practical route towards topology-enabled optical communication.

title: Trillion-scale integrated framework for high-throughput materials databases and seamless sharing
abstract: Artificial intelligence is accelerating materials discovery, yet for complex systems such as high-entropy alloys, exhaustive exploration of their immense composition spaces is computationally intractable. Here we propose an integrated framework that enables large-scale exploration with reduced resource demands. Our framework uses stateless parallel computing with message queues and containerization, and a lakehouse architecture with columnar storage and metadata-based cloud sharing. Using this framework, we constructed a ten-trillion-scale database of six-principal-element high-entropy alloys in one week, totaling 17.5 terabytes and encompassing compositions, descriptors, and predicted properties. Compared with distributed frameworks, our approach cuts runtime-memory cost by 45%, storage by 90% versus row-based formats, and accelerates subset queries up to 180 times. A full database search completes in under eight minutes using less than four gigabytes of memory. Screening over 50 billion compositions with experimental validation across two alloy families confirms the practical utility of this framework for data-driven materials discovery.

title: Game theory driven multi-agent framework mitigates language model hallucination
abstract: Lightweight large language models hold promise for scientific applications but remain limited in rule-constrained domains because they can reproduce linguistic patterns without following scientific principles, leading to hallucinations. Here, we show that G-Frame, an adaptive multi-agent framework inspired by Bayesian game and team game principles, enables a closed-loop process for automated data generation, model evaluation, and training. By assigning complementary roles to multiple agents, G-Frame generates structured reasoning data and constructs a specialized corpus containing 363,045 chain-of-thought examples and 199,589 question–answer pairs. Using this corpus together with domain pre-training and adaptive training, the 7-billion-parameter model OmniChem achieves competitive performance across the reported benchmarks and reduces the ChemJudge hallucination rate from 41.95% for the base model to 12.91%. Case studies further illustrate potential applications in molecular design and selected synthesis-planning tasks. These results support G-Frame as an extensible game theory-driven multi-agent framework for improving the reliability of lightweight scientific language models.

title: Targeting CD28 on T lineage malignancies with chimeric antigen receptor T cells
abstract: Currently, no immunotherapy is approved for T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T‑ALL). High initial response rates to CD7‑directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are limited by profound T cell aplasia and CD7‑negative immune escape, underscoring the need for alternative targets. Here, we show that CD28 is overexpressed on T‑ALL blasts from children and adolescents compared with lymphoid progenitors from healthy donors and is uniformly upregulated in nodal T-follicular helper cell lymphomas (nTFHL-AI, nTFHL-F). Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated CD28 knockout to prevent fratricide, we generate highly functional anti‑CD28 CAR T cells with selective cytotoxicity against CD28⁺ T‑ALL. Anti‑CD28 CAR T cells match anti‑CD7 CAR T cells in vitro and in vivo, but cause markedly less lymphodepletion, largely sparing CD8 T cells and NK cells while preferentially depleting CD4 T cells, particularly TH2 and TH17 subsets. These findings establish CD28 as an actionable target for CAR T cell therapy of T cell malignancies.

title: Reward function compression facilitates goal-dependent reinforcement learning
abstract: Humans can uniquely assign value to novel, abstract outcomes to support reinforcement learning. However, this flexibility is cognitively costly and reduces learning efficiency. We propose that goal-dependent learning initially relies on capacity-limited working memory. With consistent experience, learners create a compressed reward function — a simplified rule — that transfers to long-term memory for automatic evaluation upon receiving feedback. This automaticity frees working memory resources, thereby boosting learning efficiency. Across six experiments, we demonstrate that learning is impaired by the size of the goal space but improves when this space allows for compression. Additionally, faster reward processing correlates with better learning. Although the algorithmic details remain to be established, computational modeling revealed that individual differences in compression efficiency, proxied by reward processing speed, led to higher choice accuracy. Together, our behavioral results and computational models suggest that efficient goal-directed learning relies on compressing complex goals into stable reward functions.

title: Distinguishing learning asymmetry from perseveration in behavioral models
abstract: A central challenge in cognitive science is to distinguish between multiple processes that can result in similar behaviors. In reinforcement learning, one prominent example concerns two potential drivers of choice repetition: a learning asymmetry, in which agents learn differently from outcomes depending on their valence and/or whether they confirm choice, and choice perseveration, an outcome-independent tendency to repeat past choices. Evidence for asymmetric learning has typically relied on computational models that control for perseveration, or specific behavioral markers. Here, we show both these approaches have critical flaws and can spuriously detect learning asymmetries even in perseverative, symmetric-learning agents. To address this, we introduce a statistical test that distinguishes genuine learning asymmetries from spurious effects. Applying this test to a large dataset spanning ten published experiments across four studies, we find that some previously reported confirmation biases are fragile, albeit others remain robust even at an across-study level. Finally, we propose a task design that can yield a more valid qualitative signature of confirmation bias. Our approach provides a reliable framework for disentangling processes underlying choice repetition, while providing tools for the wider research community that can minimize potential spurious effects arising from process mimicry and biased parameter estimation.

title: Emergence of polarization in networks of large language model agents
abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have empowered autonomous agents to generate social networks, communicate, and form shared and diverging opinions on political issues. However, our understanding of their collective behaviours and underlying mechanisms remains incomplete. In this paper, we simulate networked systems involving thousands of LLM agents across different backbone models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, ChatGLM, Llama-3, and DeepSeek-V3), in which agents interact through LLM-guided conversations and update their opinions over time, resulting in the emergence of opinion polarization. We discover that these agents spontaneously develop their own social network with properties characteristic of human social networks, such as homophilic clustering. The collective opinions of these LLM agents evolve in ways that exhibit behavioural patterns consistent with social phenomena and mechanisms widely discussed in empirical studies of human behaviour and opinion-dynamics models. This consistency suggests that LLM agents can serve as a valuable synthetic testbed for exploring hypothetical intervention strategies in networked LLM-agent systems. Using this testbed, we further examine the effects of a range of network- and individual-level interventions, such as promoting more diverse interactions and reducing confirmation bias. Overall, this work not only sheds light on subtle opinion dynamics and collective behaviour of LLM agents from a network perspective, but also demonstrates their potential for testing hypotheses about opinion dynamics and intervention strategies.

title: Photocluster catalytic oxidation enabled by structurally precise copper-hydride nanoclusters
abstract: The utilization of light energy emerges as a prominent strategy to boost nanocluster catalysis, spurring rapid growth in the field termed photocluster catalysis. In particular, structurally well-defined copper-hydride nanoclusters attract attention as promising photocluster catalysts for organic synthesis. Herein, we report Cu 13 H 6 exhibits excellent activity for photocatalytic α -C–H oxidation, revealing great potential in oxidation chemistry. Cu 13 H 6 is one-pot synthesized and characterized using advanced analytical techniques. Critically, machine learning tentatively identifies hydride positions, reducing dependence on neutron diffraction. The Cu 13 H 6 nanocluster exhibits outstanding activity in the photooxidation of diverse alkyl aromatics and alcohols to ketones under mild conditions. This pathway also supports photocatalytic defluorination, deuteriation, cyclopropane ring-opening and dehydrogenative coupling. This work tentatively determines the structure of Cu 13 H 6 using robust stochastic surface walking global optimization with neural network, and identifies the cluster as a versatile, efficient photocatalyst that broadens photocatalysis applications in organic synthesis.

title: Long-term nitrous acid evolution modulates ozone and secondary aerosol variations in global megacities
abstract: Nitrous acid (HONO) is a crucial urban source of HO x radicals, promoting surface ozone (O 3 ) and secondary fine particle (PM 2.5 ) formation, yet its long-term evolution and air-quality impacts remain poorly constrained. Here, using a deep neural network established on worldwide field campaigns, we reconstruct global surface HONO distributions. Typical megacities exhibited contrasting trends in 2005–2021, marked by a sharp decline in Beijing (−47.4% in 2013–2021), an increase in Delhi (+10.0% in 2005–2018), and slight decreases in London, New York and Los Angeles. These HONO changes are identified as major driver of O 3 and particulate nitrate variations, outweighing contributions of conventional NO x and volatile organic compounds abatement in Beijing and Delhi, while showing comparable impacts in the remaining cities. A fused data-driven framework further uncovers regime-dependent HONO reduction strategies, prioritizing NO x control in summer and co-reduction of NO x , PM 2.5 and direct combustion emissions in winter, to accelerate O 3 and PM 2.5 joint mitigation.

title: Time-lapse RESOLFT nanoscopy empowered by deep learning
abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

title: ETSAM: effectively segmenting cell membranes in cryo-electron tomograms
abstract: Cryogenic Electron Tomography (cryo-ET) is an emerging experimental technique used to visualize cell structures and macromolecules in their native cellular environment. Accurate segmentation of cell structures in cryo-ET tomograms, such as cell membranes, supports the study of cellular organization and function. However, several inherent limitations in cryo-ET, including the very low signal-to-noise ratio, missing wedge artifacts from limited tilt angles, and other noise artifacts, collectively hinder the reliable identification and delineation of these structures. In this study, we present ETSAM, a two-stage Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2)-based fine-tuned AI method that effectively segments cell membranes in tomograms. It is trained on a diverse dataset comprising 83 experimental tomograms from the CryoET Data Portal (CDP) database and 28 simulated tomograms generated using PolNet. On an independent test set of 17 experimental tomograms for which ground-truth annotations are available, ETSAM outperforms other deep learning based methods by robustly identifying cell membranes with high sensitivity while also maintaining better precision.

title: Interpretable AI-guided discovery of degradable ionizable lipids with enhanced hepatic mRNA delivery in vivo
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) enable RNA medicines, yet ionizable-lipid discovery remains largely empirical, particularly when in vitro activity must be translated into functional hepatic delivery in vivo. Here we establish an interpretable discovery framework that combines modular degradable lipid chemistry, high-throughput phenotyping, machine learning, virtual library expansion, and independent in vivo validation to define a learnable ionizable-lipid design space. Starting from a 520-member library, we train an XGBoost model on firefly luciferase (Fluc) expression in HeLa cells and use physicochemical descriptors and molecular fingerprints to prospectively prioritize candidates with higher predicted in vitro transfection activity across a 10,920-member virtual space. In vivo phenotyping subsequently identifies PA97MD101 as a lead ionizable lipid. In mice, PA97MD101 enhances hepatic mRNA expression and Cre-dependent recombination and supports Cas9/sgTtr-mediated TTR suppression. Its performance is associated with pH-dependent membrane activity and reduced lysosomal colocalization. These findings support further evaluation of PA97MD101 for functional hepatic RNA delivery.

title: NiCLIP: neuroimaging contrastive language-image pretraining model for predicting text from brain activation images
abstract: Predicting cognitive processes from brain activation maps remains a key challenge in neuroscience. Meta-analytic functional decoding provides an estimation of behavioral profiles associated with specific brain regions; however, existing methods fail to capture the full semantic content of the neuroimaging literature. To address this, we present NiCLIP, a contrastive language-image model trained on over 23,000 articles to predict cognitive tasks, concepts, and domains from brain activation patterns. NiCLIP achieves optimal performance when using full-text articles and a curated cognitive ontology with precise task-concept-domain mappings. Our results show that NiCLIP accurately predicts cognitive tasks from Human Connectome Project group-level maps across multiple domains (e.g., emotion, language, motor) and precisely characterizes the functional roles of specific brain regions, including the amygdala, hippocampus, and temporoparietal junction. However, NiCLIP showed limitations with noisy subject-level activation maps. NiCLIP represents a significant advancement in functional decoding, offering a powerful tool for hypothesis generation and scientific discovery.

title: Reinforcement learning guided robotic platform that investigates and discovers asymmetric reactions
abstract: Autonomous robotic platforms accelerate chemical discovery by coupling automated experimentation with algorithmic decision-making, but most lack integrated support for chirality and the sequential decision-making required to explore asymmetric reaction spaces with unknown reactivity and stereochemical outcomes. Here, we report a bespoke robotic platform guided by deep reinforcement learning that autonomously navigates a defined asymmetric reaction space by scouting reaction conditions, discovering chiral products, screening catalysts and mapping substrate scope. The structure-agnostic workflow is enabled by a digital twin of asymmetric catalysis, in which control policies are trained before transfer to the laboratory. We validate the approach in chiral phosphoric acid catalysis: over 30 days, the system made more than 3,000 decisions and uncovered four highly enantioselective transformations, including an axially chiral molecule and three allene syntheses, one involving the enantioselective functionalization of a pyrrolopyrrole moiety. These results highlight deep reinforcement learning-guided autonomy as a strategy for discovery in complex catalytic systems.

title: Wireless, optoelectronic, multimodal skin sensor for simultaneous monitoring of mechanical stress and vascular responses
abstract: Prolonged mechanical loading and subsequent vascular ischemia drive the development of severe pressure injuries. Effective prevention of irreversible tissue damage requires monitoring both multiaxial mechanical forces and physiological erythema. However, conventional diagnostic tools remain limited by rigid architectures, single parameter detection, and subjective visual assessments. Here, a wireless, battery free optoelectronic multimodal sensor platform provides an integrated framework for tracking posture dependent mechanical loading and localized erythema. The soft, skin conformable device uses geometric light modulation within an isolated optical cavity to quantify normal pressure and biaxial shear stresses. To resolve complex mechanical environments, a deep neural network regression model decouples simultaneous tri-axial forces, Fx, Fy, and Fz, at the skin interface. Concurrently, a dual wavelength optical reflectance mechanism quantifies skin erythema by capturing subtle variations in hemoglobin absorption. Opaque elastomeric encapsulation shields the internal optics, supporting stable optical measurements under varying ambient illumination and skin conditions. System level integration via near field communication enables untethered operation across a multiplexed sensor network. On-body evaluations in a simulated clinical bed setting demonstrate the ability of the platform to dynamically map posture-dependent biomechanical loading and localized vascular responses, providing a technological basis for future studies on data-driven monitoring of the mechanical and vascular factors associated with pressure-injury risk.

title: Small viruses reveal bidirectional evolution between HK97-fold viruses and encapsulins via procapsids
abstract: The HK97-fold is an ancient, conserved protein structure that assembles protein shells, forming the capsids of Duplodnaviria viruses and prokaryotic biochemical compartments called encapsulsins. It has been proposed that encapsulins evolved from HK97-fold viruses. But the higher complexity of viral capsids represents a biophysical paradox in the evolution of HK97-fold protein shells. To resolve this problem, we hypothesize the existence of simpler HK97-fold viral capsids associated with smaller genomes than those of known HK97-fold viruses. Such small viral genomes are searched in environmental metagenomes across public databases, including IMG/M and MGnify. Using hidden Markov models and protein language models, we identify and characterize small viral genomes encoding HK97-fold proteins that exhibit molecular similarities to encapsulins yet lack portal and tail genes. The phylogenetic analyses of HK97-fold proteins reveal independent mixed groups of viruses and encapsulins, and structural analyses identify similarities between encapsulins and procapsids, the immature state of viral capsids. The observations support a bidirectional evolution between encapsulins and HK97-fold viruses enabled by the viral procapsid state. Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions.

title: Mapping cell-type-specific spatial gene programs uncovers tissue architecture and microenvironment organization
abstract: The complex organization of tissues is shaped by the spatial arrangement of diverse cell types executing specialized gene programs. Cell-type-specific spatial gene programs (SGPs) are transcriptional modules that capture spatial expression co-variation within cell types. However, identifying these SGPs remains challenging in spatial transcriptomics. Here we present MacSGP, a scalable framework that integrates deep graph neural networks with probabilistic modeling to identify cell-type-specific SGPs through low-rank structures while accounting for cell type mixtures. Through comprehensive simulations and real data analyses spanning diverse tissues and technologies, we demonstrate that MacSGP effectively distinguishes cell-type-specific SGPs from cell-type marker gene expression patterns while uncovering tissue architecture and cellular microenvironments. In a mouse brain dataset, we identify replicable SGPs reflecting subregional neuronal specializations, with these genes significantly enriched for heritabilities associated with brain-related phenotypes. Across colorectal cancer datasets from various platforms, MacSGP identifies consistent SGPs that define distinct cellular niches within the tumor microenvironment.

title: Machine-learning surrogates enable rapid prediction of 3-D substrate gradients in industrial bioreactors
abstract: High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) provide detailed substrate gradient predictions in industrial stirred-tank bioreactors but are computationally intensive, limiting their routine application. We developed surrogate models trained on \(760\) CFD simulations to rapidly predict fully 3-D substrate concentration fields from global operating conditions (e.g., stirring speed, feeding strategy, feeding point location, fluid density and viscosity, liquid height, bio-kinetic parameters, biomass concentration), and local spatial descriptors (e.g., distance to the feeding point). Among various methods, attention-based neural networks achieved the highest accuracy (test \({{{\rm{R}}}}^{2}\approx 0.91\) ), capturing essential mixing features and enabling millisecond-scale inference—up to a million-fold speed-up compared to CFD. These surrogates facilitate rapid exploration of operating spaces, supporting real-time optimization and digital-twin frameworks in bioprocessing. Our results demonstrate that data-driven models can effectively couple hydrodynamics and biokinetics to provide fast, accurate spatial predictions, advancing capabilities for industrial bioreactor design and control.

title: Dendritic computation bridges neuroscience and foundation models
abstract: A prevailing view holds that although neuroscience historically inspired AI, its role in the recent evolution of AI, driven by the scaling of foundation models, is minor. We challenge this perspective by establishing a biological analogy between simplified dendritic neuron models and the attention mechanisms central to AI foundation models. We show that AI attention mechanisms bear direct mappings to internal neuronal complexities arising from dendritic organization, rather than to the mere inter-neuronal connections of simple point neurons. This re-conceptualization not only offers a neuroscience-informed perspective for understanding core AI methodologies beyond their formulation as abstract mathematical operations, but also paves the way for neuro-inspired foundation models that leverage neuroscientific insights to sustainably advance modern AI beyond scaling laws. As an example of this paradigm, we introduce a dendritic-inspired complexity framework, and design a hybrid-attention foundation model with dendritic-inspired sparse computation, which enhances memory capacity while reducing computational demands. Our model supports a 50M context window-equivalent to roughly 40 volumes of Shakespeare-demonstrating superior long-term memory capabilities. This work pioneers a paradigm that harnesses intra-neuronal dynamics to drive sustained advances in modern AI, while also offering a potential route to understanding dendritic computational mechanisms.

title: Spatial targeting and expansion prevention offer effective pathways to protect African maize from parasitic weeds
abstract: Parasitic weeds ( Striga spp.) threaten food security for over 300 million Africans dependent on maize, yet economic impact estimates vary widely due to high uncertainties, limiting strategic planning and interventions. We developed a spatially-explicit framework overcoming data scarcity through integrated agroecological similarity mapping, machine learning, and stochastic modeling to quantify Striga economic impacts across African maize production systems. Our analysis resolves decades of uncertainty, revealing annual losses of US$1.04 billion (95% confidence interval: US$0.94–1.15 billion) with high spatial concentration: less than 6% of infested areas generate half the economic losses. Agricultural expansion represents the primary future risk, potentially tripling losses by 2050 as Striga colonizes new areas. Interventions achieve maximum impact through a dual strategy: spatial targeting of high-loss zones coupled with prevention in agricultural expansion areas. This targeted approach outperforms uniform intensification, providing a blueprint for managing agricultural pests in data-scarce regions.

title: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
abstract: Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence reveals spatially divergent effects of global change on mammals
abstract: Understanding how global change reshapes species distributions remains a central challenge in ecology, yet most global assessments treat environmental drivers as static, uniform, or aggregate influences. This obscures where, why, and how specific drivers generate ecological risk or opportunity. Here, we apply explainable machine learning to assess how climate averages, variability, extremes, and land cover are projected to reshape future distributions of 1,992 terrestrial mammals. Using Shapley Additive Explanations with species distribution models, we quantify the directional contribution of 16 environmental drivers and track how these contributions change over space and time. We propose two ecological diagnostics, directional turnovers and favorability shifts, that reveal where drivers switch from favorable to unfavorable, or the reverse, and where their influence strengthens or weakens without sign reversal. While not designed to infer causation, our framework assesses whether projected spatial patterns align with ecological expectations. We show that climate extremes impose intense but spatially restricted impacts, temperature-related drivers dominate exposure patterns, particularly for specialist species, and the same driver can impose risk in one region while creating opportunity in another. By decomposing projected biodiversity change into driver-specific signatures, our framework advances biodiversity forecasting toward a more actionable understanding of ecological risk and opportunity.

title: LitGene: an interpretable transformer model integrating text and ontology for gene representation learning
abstract: Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Here, we present LitGene, an interpretable transformer-based model that refines gene representations by integrating unstructured textual information with Gene Ontology annotations through contrastive learning. In evaluations across eight benchmark tasks for protein properties, LitGene achieves competitive accuracy and exhibits zero-shot prediction of GO terms, KEGG pathways, and gene-disease associations. LitGene identified ANGPTL6 as a potential candidate gene for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), supported by its differential expression in independent IPF samples, illustrating LitGene’s utility for hypothesis generation. A SHAP-based interpretability tool highlights text features influencing predictions, while an automated literature-grounding framework provides corroborating support where available. Our results suggest that integrating textual and genetic information may help reduce biases associated with under-studied genes. The model is released as open-source code, along with a publicly accessible web interface at https://litgene.cs.unm.edu/ , which allows users to submit gene names, disease names, drug names, or custom text (e.g., publication abstracts) to obtain evidence-based predictions of related biomedical entities.

title: Fluke-borne viruses are a risk factor and diagnostic target for diseases caused by carcinogenic trematodes
abstract: Three trematode parasites, Schistosoma haematobium , Opisthorchis viverrini , and Clonorchis sinensis are recognized group 1 carcinogens for their roles in squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder and bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma). We aimed to assess the presence of fluke viruses and their association with malignancy in fluke infections. We showed that all three carcinogenic trematodes harbored related viruses. Focusing on O. viverrini , we observed virus persistence at discrete life stages and viral tropism for the fluke tegument, and we provided molecular and serological evidence of parasitized hosts’ exposure to viral RNA and proteins. Serological analyses confirmed seroconversion of residents in endemic sites and revealed that antibody titers and avidity against fluke-borne viruses increase in individuals with hepatobiliary diseases. Random forest models discriminated efficiently between liver-fluke-infected participants without disease and those with periductal fibrosis or cholangiocarcinoma. Thus, we show that fluke-borne viruses are risk factors and diagnostic targets for fluke-associated cancer.

title: Permeability heterogeneity controls fluid migration and microseismicity evolution in The Geysers geothermal field, California
abstract: Fracture networks directly govern the efficiency of geothermal energy extraction and play a critical role in fluid migration and microearthquake generation. Using deep learning and Markov clustering, we build a high-resolution microseismic catalog covering the past decade for The Geysers geothermal field, California. Our observations reveal distinctive clustering patterns and inferred fracture systems tightly correlated with injection operations. Source mechanism analyses and pore pressure simulations indicate that the inferred connected fracture network provides pathways for rapid and directional pore pressure diffusion, highlighting that heterogeneous permeability controls the localized migration of fluids and the associated microseismic response. Our study highlights the importance of continuous and integrated seismic monitoring for ensuring the sustainability of long-term reservoir development and exploitation.

title: De novo design of lipopeptides with antimicrobial potency enabled by a chain-as-prompt deep learning framework
abstract: Antimicrobial lipopeptides (AMLPs) represent a promising solution to global antibiotic crisis, yet their precision design remains challenging due to the inability of current computational models to account for N -terminal fatty acid modification. Here we develop a deep learning-driven AMLP model for de novo design of AMLPs by integrating a chain-as-prompt mechanism with domain-adaptive transfer learning, effectively bridging the representation gap between peptide sequence and lipid-induced bioactivity. Using the AMLP model, 2657 evolutionarily selected RiPP-derived core peptide sequences from 96,911 bacterial genomes are inspiringly designed for virtual lipidation with seven N -terminal fatty acid chains (C6–C18) followed by predictive screening, generating 6197 candidate sequences. Notably, we find that both high KRH rate ( ≥ 0.3) and common fatty acid tails (C12 and C16) are also critical for further selection of candidate AMLPs, resulting in 289 sequences. Then, 46 are randomly synthesized, with 44 showing antimicrobial activities (a positive rate of 95.7%). The lead antibiotic LP630 exhibits broad-spectrum activities against typical Gram-positive, Gram-negative and mycobacterial strains by targeting multiple bacterial cell membrane components, and demonstrates potent therapeutic efficacy in murine wound infection models. Our study provides a streamlined and universal paradigm for deep learning-enabled high-throughput discovery of novel lipopeptide therapeutics.

title: Projected intensification of soil salinization in global drylands under future aridity increase
abstract: Soil salinization threatens agricultural production, water management, and ecosystem health. Yet, how increasing aridity will reshape 21st-century soil salinity patterns across drylands, particularly in croplands, remains unclear. Here, we compile a relatively comprehensive global soil salinity dataset from the past two decades, projecting future dryland soil salinity dynamics using climate-driven machine learning models with multiple covariates, including dynamic dryland extent and human influences. Our results show an 8% expansion of global drylands saline soils under increasing aridity by 2100 (SSP5-8.5) relative to 2004–2023. Southwestern US, Mexico, southern Europe, central South America, eastern and southern Africa are highest-risk hotspots. We further show dryland croplands face serious salinization, especially irrigated systems, where half of these newly salinized areas project more than 4.9% (maize), 17.2% (dryland rice), 3.3% (sorghum), and 21.2% (wheat) potential production losses. Our findings inform long-term adaptation strategies to mitigate emerging salinization risks and sustain water and food security.

title: Closed-loop photoreactor design enabled by machine learning and digital twins
abstract: Designing efficient photoreactors remains challenging due to the complex interplay of reflection, scattering, and absorption. Here, we introduce a closed-loop workflow integrating ray-tracing digital twins with multi-objective Bayesian optimization to design photoreactors with high photon capture and uniform irradiation. A digital 3D reactor model is calibrated using measured emission characteristics, reflectivity data, and geometrical properties and validated against potassium ferrioxalate actinometry. The validated model explores reflector shape and vial positioning, identifying geometries that maximize incident photon flux while maintaining homogeneity across 16 vials. Experimental validation using a photocatalytic Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling shows that reaction yields track simulated photon flux. The optimized reactor is further applied to quantum-yield screening, enabling mechanistic insights across diverse conditions in a single experiment. This work establishes an experimentally validated virtual co-design framework in which machine learning and digital twins accelerate photoreactor development and support quantitative understanding of photochemical processes.

title: Ten protein panel predicts ALS from plasma with high accuracy
abstract: Predictive biomarkers are increasingly used to guide clinical trial design, diagnosis, and management of patients with neurodegenerative diseases. We profiled plasma from 632 ALS patients and 160 healthy controls using the NULISA CNS and Inflammation Panels and applied eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) with nested cross-validation and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to identify disease-associated proteins. A 12-protein candidate panel was refined using SHAP feature importance and absolute quantification, then evaluated in an independent validation cohort (144 ALS, 37 controls). We identified a final 10-protein panel (NEFL, FOLR1, pTau-181, TREM1, VEGFA, NEFH, CALCA, NRGN, LAMP3, and PTX3) that achieved high classification performance (balanced accuracy 98.3%; AUC 0.992). Model performance was driven by plasma proteomic signatures rather than clinical variables and was not dependent on neurofilament light chain alone. Representing over 750 ALS cases, this study supports development of a clinically deployable blood-based ALS screening tool.

title: Three-photon population imaging of subcortical brain regions
abstract: Monitoring large-scale neuronal activity in deep brain circuits is crucial for understanding the principles of brain function. However, existing large-scale cellular-resolution imaging techniques are limited in imaging depth and cannot monitor activity in areas deeper than the cortex in the intact brain. To address this challenge, we developed a Large Imaging Field of view Three-photon (LIFT) microscope with a FOV of > 3 mm 2 . LIFT combines high-numerical-aperture optimized sampling, using a custom scanning module, with deep learning-based denoising, to enable population imaging in subcortical brain regions of mice and deep cortical regions of rats. We demonstrate calcium imaging in the intact mouse brain from more than 1500 cells across CA1, the surrounding white matter, and adjacent deep layers of the cortex, and show population imaging with high SNR at a depth of 1.2 mm in the rat cortex. The LIFT microscope offers versatility in imaging scale and rate and was built entirely from off-the-shelf components.

title: Large-scale proteomic characterization reveals clinically relevant subtypes of early-stage papillary thyroid cancer for prognostic prediction
abstract: Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) has a rising incidence. The majority are diagnosed at an early stage, albeit with a minority exhibiting aggressive tendencies. Given its generally indolent nature, controversy persists regarding the management of early-stage PTCs, particularly surgical intervention and long-term surveillance strategies. Here, we conduct a large-scale proteomic characterization of early-stage PTC based on tumor samples from 797 patients. Proteomic profiling unveils clinically relevant modules and identifies six subtypes, capturing the spectrum of heterogeneity from indolent to progressive disease states. Notably, subtypes associated with higher progression risk display enhanced signatures of ribogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Furthermore, integrating machine learning with protein co-expression network analysis, we identify predictive markers of PTC progression risk such as GPX3 and TMSB4X. Integration of clinical and proteomic data provides a valuable resource for a deeper understanding of early-stage PTC biology and may inform personalized management strategies for patients with indolent or progressive disease.

title: High-risk antimicrobial resistance genomic traits in multidrug-resistant Salmonella across China’s food chain: projections to 2050
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rising globally, yet factors shaping its genomic evolution remain poorly understood. We investigated how socioeconomic, climate, and health factors are associated with AMR spread in multi-drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella enterica across China’s food chain, mapped hotspots and forecasted genomic trait prevalence to 2050. We analysed 2,536 MDR genomes from 15 provinces over 16 years, covering patients, food and non-food workers, meat, livestock, and environmental sources. A machine learning framework integrated genomic surveillance with risk assessment to identify high-risk AMR traits (clinically relevant, MDR, mobile). Regression models linked trait prevalence to socioeconomic, climate, health, and antimicrobial consumption data, informing projections to 2050. Eighty-four high-risk traits, including carbapenem, colistin, and β-lactam resistance, are projected to rise, with antibiotic use, population growth, healthcare spending, and urbanisation. Projections were trait-specific: bla CTX-M-64 and bla TEM-1 may increase up to 20%, while bla CTX-M-65 and bla CTX-M-14 remain below 5%. A mechanistic shift in fluoroquinolone resistance is projected: mutation-based resistance ( gyrA 87) declines while plasmid-mediated genes ( qnrB17 , qnrS1 ) rise. Food workers emerged as a potential reservoir, showing higher trait prevalence than food sources, uniquely carrying last-resort antibiotic-resistance genes ( bla TEM-30 , bla NDM-5 , bla CTX-M-64 ). Integrating genomic with socioeconomic surveillance could shift AMR interventions from reactive to preventive.

title: HRDPath: an explainable multi-model deep learning architecture for predicting homologous recombination deficiency from histopathology images
abstract: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is a critical biomarker for guiding treatment decisions in high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), a cancer with few reliable biomarkers. However, existing genomics-based tests for HRD are variable, expensive, and time-consuming. We develop HRDPath, a patient-level deep learning architecture that predicts HRD status from whole slide images, requiring no additional molecular testing. HRDPath is validated across three cohorts of female patients and achieves an AUC of 0.846, significantly outperforming previously reported results in HGSOC. By incorporating multiple slides per patient and targeted optimization strategies, we strengthen the model clinical utility, with both specificity and sensitivity reaching 0.90. Our interpretability pipeline enhances model trustworthiness and reveals important clinical and biological insights into HRD-positive cancers, highlighting the associated morphological and pathological changes at the cellular and tissue levels. HRDPath provides a foundation for an accessible and scalable digital biomarker to improve treatment stratification in ovarian cancer globally.

title: Structural basis of TACO1 function in mitochondrial translation elongation
abstract: Protein synthesis depends on specialized regulatory factors to overcome difficult-to-translate sequences during elongation that cause ribosomal stalling. In human mitochondria, this function is carried out by TACO1 (Translation activator of COX1). Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structure of human TACO1 bound to the mitoribosome, revealing its mechanistic role as a dedicated elongation regulator. Unlike the prokaryotic elongation factor EF-P and the eukaryotic eIF5A, which bind the ribosomal E site and stabilize P-site tRNA to facilitate peptide bond formation, TACO1 adopts a distinct strategy. It binds near the A site, closely interacting with the Sarcin Ricin loop and the L7/L12 stalk, similar to general translation elongation factors, such as EF-Tumt and mtEF-G1mt, and contacts the A-site tRNA. Using AlphaFold analysis and molecular dynamics simulations, we further show how a series of conformational changes allow its N-terminal domain to reorient and transiently engage with the A-site tRNA via a conserved and functionally critical basic amino acid patch. The bacterial homolog of TACO1, namely YebC2, shares the structural features required for its function. Overall, we present an evolutionarily conserved mechanism employed by TACO1 to enhance mitochondrial translation efficiency.

title: Reduced-DSP 200G/λ low-voltage slow-light silicon modulator enabled by built-in EO equalizer
abstract: Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer. By monolithically integrating optical delay lines and crossings within segmented slow-light phase shifters, we synthesized an on-chip feedforward response that extends the 3-dB bandwidth. The fabricated modulator with a small device length of 320 µm demonstrated 140-Gb/s on-off keying operation with an energy consumption of 26 fJ/bit using drive voltages compatible with fin field-effect transistor-based complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology. Furthermore, four-level pulse amplitude modulation achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing and 200 Gb/s with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. By reducing reliance on power-dissipating electronics, this strategy provides a potential route toward future dense multi-Tb/s co-packaged optics for energy-constrained switching systems.

title: Molecular basis of coupled peptidoglycan synthesis by the FtsWIQLB divisome complex from Vibrio cholerae
abstract: Bacterial cell division requires synchronized synthesis of septal peptidoglycan by the glycosyltransferase FtsW and the transpeptidase FtsI within the divisome. How glycan polymerization and peptide crosslinking are coordinated within this assembly remains poorly understood. Here, we provide molecular insights into this coupling in the core divisome complex FtsWIQLB from Vibrio cholerae . By integrating a quantitative, native substrates-based dual-activity assay, cryo-EM, AlphaFold modeling, disulfide trapping, mass spectrometry, and chemical biology, we identify an inactive down and a putative active up conformation of FtsI with distinct interaction networks. We discover a coupling helix in FtsI that directly modulates FtsW processivity. Importantly, crosslinking requires a minimum glycan strand length, consistent with our model of coupling. Lastly, the lipid tail of lipid II is important for FtsW processivity, with short-tail analogs acting as inhibitors. Our findings suggest that substrate-driven conformational switching of FtsI spatially and temporally couples these essential enzymatic activities.

title: Unveiling the functional specialisation of human white matter circuits with naturalistic stimuli
abstract: Functional MRI (fMRI) has traditionally focused on grey matter activations, overlooking the contribution of white matter pathways to brain organisation. Yet evidence suggests that white matter constrains, modulates, and integrates signals across distant regions. Here, we introduce a framework to map the functional specialisation of white matter circuits using fMRI scans collected while participants watched naturalistic videos. By leveraging ecologically valid stimuli, this method captures cognition as it naturally unfolds. Integrating fMRI with brain connections, we derived a functionally grounded parcellation of the connectome, challenging conventional cortical-based cognitive taxonomy. Distinct cognitive profiles emerged for association and commissural fibres, with association pathways preferentially linked to language-related processes and commissural pathways to executive and motor functions, affirming the functionally heterogeneous nature of white matter systems. An artificial intelligence framework applied to independent datasets confirmed the robustness and functional relevance of the identified parcels. This open-access framework also enables the interactive exploration of white matter functional organisation, offering a new lens on the neural bases of cognition.

title: Small molecule biomarkers predictive of Chagas disease progression
abstract: Chagas disease (CD), caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi , affects an estimated 10.5 million people worldwide and remains a leading cause of infectious cardiomyopathy in Latin America. Although infection is lifelong without treatment, only 20–30% of chronically infected individuals progress from an asymptomatic stage to clinically significant cardiac disease, and current antiparasitic therapies are limited by toxicity and variable efficacy. Reliable biomarkers capable of predicting disease progression would improve clinical risk stratification and support therapeutic development. Here, we performed a metabolomics study to identify serum biomarkers predictive of progression from asymptomatic infection to cardiac CD. Untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry profiling using complementary chromatographic platforms and univariate statistics, machine learning feature selection, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis were performed to identify candidate biomarkers. These biomarkers were validated by targeted analysis. We identified eight individual metabolite biomarkers and 45 combinatorial panels predictive of progression status, including 10 panels that met sensitivity and specificity criteria defined in the target product profile for CD treatment-response biomarkers. These findings demonstrate that circulating metabolites measured at baseline can predict future cardiac disease progression and provide a foundation for clinically deployable prognostic tools in chronic Chagas disease.

title: Chemistry-infused bandit framework for interpretable autonomous campaign of electrocatalysis
abstract: Autonomous experimentation offers a time-efficient route towards accelerated catalyst discovery, but current practices often rely on black-box models that are difficult to interpret. Here we demonstrate the paradigm of interpretable autonomous exploration of a 12-dimensional space in the electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction by integrating an interpretable decision-making artificial intelligence with a fully automated electrochemical platform. Guided by a human’s chemistry-informed hypothesis, a chemistry-infused bandit is established to reflect the locally quadratic approximation between synthetic conditions and electrocatalytic activities near the explored optimum region. Not only does such a decision-making bandit lead to the discovery of previously unreported, earth-abundant electrocatalysts at least comparable to Pt-based ones, the bandit also reveals model-derived hypothesis for how synthetic conditions affect the electrocatalysts’ performance near the identified local optima as autonomous inquiry proceeds, which is otherwise untenable from black-box ones. Incorporating chemistry-informed hypothesis into the decision-making bandit is generally applicable to any chemistry problem and offers a framework for autonomous investigation, advancing hypothesis generation for catalyst’s design principles beyond simple optimization.

title: Predicting follow-up cognition using estimated structural and functional connectivity networks and artificial intelligence in multiple sclerosis
abstract: Brain’s structural and functional connectomes (SC and FC) offer insights into the relationship between brain circuits and cognitive functioning in people with multiple sclerosis (MS). However, diffusion and functional MRI, which are used to extract SC and FC, is expensive and time consuming, therefore are not currently used in the clinical setting. Our prior work demonstrated that estimated SC and FC (eSC and eFC) generated using MS lesion masks and artificial intelligence (AI) models can predict disability as effectively as SC and FC derived from diffusion and functional MRI in MS. In this study, we identify the eSC and eFC brain circuits that are associated with baseline and 4-year follow-up cognition and assess the ability of eSC and eFC in predicting cognition in MS. In a cohort of 171 with MS, the Network Modification tool was performed to estimate SC from the MS lesion mask, which is extracted from structural MRI scans. The eSC was then used as an input to Krakencoder, an encoder-decoder model, to estimate FC. The highest accuracy was obtained when predicting follow-up Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) using regional eSC or eFC, with a median Spearman’s correlation coefficient of 0.58 for eSC and 0.56 for eFC. Decreased eSC and eFC in the cerebellum and increased eFC in the default mode network were associated with lower follow-up SDMT scores. Our findings demonstrate that eSC and eFC derived from clinically acquired MRI and AI models can effectively predict cognition. The use of lesion-based estimates of connectomes may potentially inform clinical trials by identifying the specific brain circuits that could be targeted for the non-invasive treatments aimed at improving cognitive function in MS.

title: Spin-adapted neural network wavefunctions in real space
abstract: Spin plays a fundamental role in understanding electronic structure, yet many real-space wavefunction methods fail to adequately consider it. We introduce the spin-adapted antisymmetrization method, a general procedure that enforces exact total spin symmetry for antisymmetric many-electron wavefunctions in real space. In the context of neural network-based quantum Monte Carlo, our method leverages the expressiveness of deep neural networks to capture electron correlation while enforcing exact spin adaptation via group representation theory. This framework provides a principled route to embed physical priors into otherwise black-box neural network wavefunctions, yielding a compact representation of correlated systems with neural network orbitals. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we study the spin ladder of iron-sulfur clusters, a long-standing challenge for many-body methods due to their dense spectrum of nearly degenerate spin states. Our results reveal accurate resolution of low-lying spin states and spin gaps in [Fe 2 S 2 ] and [Fe 4 S 4 ] clusters, offering insights into their electronic structures. In sum, these findings establish our framework as a practical route toward spin-adapted neural network-based quantum Monte Carlo for strongly correlated systems.

title: Predicting protein electrostatics with protein language models
abstract: Ionization states are crucial to protein function, yet predicting their equilibrium constants remains challenging. Here we present KaML-ESMs, sequence-based neural networks built on the ESM protein language models and trained on the GAINES-augmented PKAD-3r dataset. KaML-ESM2/ESMC outperform alternative approaches across four benchmarks, achieving root-mean-square errors of about 0.5 units for Asp/Glu/His/Cys/Tyr/Lys residues in native proteins. Performance degrades on 89 buried engineered mutations lacking evolutionary support, revealing a limitation that supervised training may help overcome. These results suggest that protein sequence, through its evolutionary context, encodes not only structure and function but also, indirectly, electrostatic characteristics. Applying KaML-ESM2 to the entire human proteome, we show that predicted p K a values can identify functional sites and infer catalytic mechanisms. We offer KaML, a sequence-based p K a prediction platform supporting biological exploration, protein engineering, and biomolecular simulation. With further development, GAINES could provide a general framework for addressing data scarcity in machine learning.

title: Recommendation system-inspired learning of crossmodal interaction patterns between chromatin accessibility and gene expression
abstract: Despite the growing availability of crossmodal single-cell sequencing, existing approaches are limited by underutilization of biological attributes, sparse modality signals, and insufficient modeling of regulatory interactions, limiting generalization in data-scarce settings and the discovery of peak-gene-level relationships. Interestingly, such challenges mirror those in recommendation systems, where side information, high sparsity, binary interactions, and cold start problems are extensively studied. Inspired by recommender models that infer user-item preferences from incomplete interaction graphs, we present CrossRec, which reformulates scATAC and scRNA data as an interaction graph to learn regulatory patterns across single-cell tasks. Its biologically-driven bipartite graph transformer learns interpretable attention over ATAC-RNA pairs. CrossRec outperforms existing methods across various tasks, remains robust under data-scarce settings, generalizes to unseen cell types and datasets, and enhances prior-based methods. Its learned regulatory maps provide cell- and cell-type-specific insights, resolving dynamic regulatory rewiring during cortical neurogenesis and perturbation-specific rewiring of drug-induced regulation in melanoma resistance.

title: Reliability-based arbitration reveals heterogeneous model-based and model-free reinforcement learning strategies linked to compulsivity and impulsivity
abstract: The mechanisms by which humans arbitrate between reinforcement-learning strategies remain poorly understood, and the nature of these strategies has come under recent debate. Using a modified two-step decision task in two independent samples ( N = 452 and N = 226), here we show that humans integrate three forms of reliability information when arbitrating control: transition reliability, model-free reward-prediction reliability, and model-based reward-prediction reliability. These mechanisms are deployed differently across individuals, revealing predominantly model-free, model-based, mixed, and non-reinforcement learning behavioral profiles that are associated with distinct compulsivity and impulsivity profiles. Critically, individuals also differ in what they arbitrate over: some switch between model-based and model-free control, whereas others maintain model-based control while arbitrating between alternative task representations. Together, these findings reveal broad heterogeneity in human reinforcement learning and provide deeper insight into individual differences in cognition and neuropsychiatric vulnerability.

title: Emergence of diffusion models from associative memory through memorization and generalization
abstract: Dense Associative Memories (DenseAMs) are generalizations of Hopfield networks that store training data at local minima of the energy landscape. When the amount of training data exceeds the critical memory storage capacity, new local minima (different from the training data) emerge. These emergent local minima, known as spurious states, can hinder memory retrieval. We examine diffusion models (DMs) through the DenseAM lens, viewing their generative process as an attempt of a memory retrieval. In the small data regime, DMs create distinct attractors for each training sample, akin to DenseAMs below the critical capacity. As the training set size increases, DMs transition to generalization. We identify a critical intermediate phase, predicted by DenseAM theory, characterized by the emergence of spurious states. In generative modeling, these previously overlooked states are no longer negative artifacts but rather are the first signs of generative capabilities. Their existence is demonstrated across a wide range of architectures and datasets.

title: Multiproperty optimization of therapeutic antibodies through sequence editing via large language model and reinforcement learning
abstract: Discovering antibodies with multiple beneficial properties is essential for therapeutic drug development, but experimentally identified antibodies require further optimization. Joint optimization remains challenging because sequence space is vast, annotations are sparse and property tradeoffs are common. Herein, we propose AbOptimizer, a reinforcement learning framework for multiproperty antibody optimization through parallel multisite sequence editing. AbOptimizer identifies promising editing sites and edit actions, including ‘reservation’, ‘substitution’ and optional ‘insertion’ or ‘deletion’, before recommending mutations from protein language models, while surrogate evaluation and Pareto rewards shape policy training. We evaluate AbOptimizer on three therapeutic antibodies across multiproperty, data-limited and indel-inclusive optimization. In silico, AbOptimizer improves optimized properties and outperforms baseline methods. In vitro, selected variants show affinity-specificity co-optimization for emibetuzumab, improved affinity and specificity with largely maintained thermal stability for siltuximab, and indel-inclusive affinity optimization for trastuzumab. These results validate AbOptimizer as a practical framework for therapeutic antibody optimization.

title: Cephalopod-inspired embodied camouflage system for simultaneous evasion of artificial and human visual perception
abstract: Differences in visual perception mechanisms between biological and artificial intelligence make it difficult to design camouflage that is both visually natural and effective against modern detectors. Existing adversarial approaches often create conspicuous patterns and are typically static, limiting their use in dynamic real-world scenarios. Here we present CephCam, an embodied closed-loop camouflage system that integrates environment-aware color extraction, optimization-based texture generation that jointly balances visual naturalness and detector evasion, and angle-aware display compensation for physical deployment. This system involves an eye-brain-skin framework of sensing, computation, and display, motivated by the naturally evolved cephalopod camouflage, but implemented with specialized cameras, computing modules, and OLED screens on a model vehicle. CephCam targets simultaneous evasion of both human observers and modern object detectors across diverse digital and physical environments, significantly outperforming strong baselines targeting either alone. These findings underscore shared vulnerabilities in human and artificial visual processing systems, showcasing CephCam’s potential for robust, adaptive, and embodied camouflage applications.

title: Comparative analysis of end-to-end learning and foundation models for clinical-grade prostate pathology
abstract: Foundation models (FMs) using self-supervised pre-training are widely advocated as a universal solution for pathology, yet their advantages over task-specific (TS) models remain unclear. Here we show, using over 100,000 prostate biopsies from 6268 patients across 15 sites, that while FMs demonstrate utility in data-scarce scenarios, their performance converges with—and is in some cases surpassed by—TS models with sufficient labeled training data. Concordance with pathologists’ grading reaches quadratic Cohen’s kappas of 0.91 (95% CI 0.90-0.92; all models) on internal and 0.87 (0.86-0.88; TS), 0.86 (0.84-0.87; UNI FM) and 0.85 (0.84-0.86; Virchow2 FM) on external cohorts at full training. Task-specific training markedly reduces misgrading, misdiagnosis of challenging morphologies, and technical variability. Notably, FMs consume up to 35 times more energy. We advocate for considering both FMs and end-to-end learning for robust, resource-efficient, and clinically applicable AI pathology.

title: Synthesis-by-design of ferroelectric Dion–Jacobson two-dimensional hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites
abstract: Dion–Jacobson two-dimensional hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites are promising ferroelectric materials, combining chemically tunable polarity enabled by their organic spacers with enhanced environmental stability. However, rational discovery remains difficult owing to uncertain phase formability and scarce, biased ferroelectric data. Here we show a staged, physically guided synthesis-by-design workflow that integrates learning from scarce ferroelectric data with structure-aware screening. Starting from 11 known ferroelectric compounds in this family, symbolic regression defines a descriptor-bounded ferroelectric-consistent region. Similarity-guided expansion and chemical filtering reduce 83,924 molecules to 1012 candidate divalent spacers, while machine-learned interatomic-potential relaxation and connectivity analysis identify 338 candidates retaining Dion–Jacobson connectivity. Sequential prioritization by connectivity retention, chemical similarity, energetic refinement and synthetic accessibility selects s −2-fluorobutane-1,4-diamine, leading to the synthesis of a PbI 4 -based Dion–Jacobson perovskite with experimentally confirmed ferroelectric switching. This prospective proof of concept shows how sparse property knowledge can be coupled with structural screening to prioritize organic spacer candidates for experimental synthesis.

title: scBOA: Bayesian optimization of single-cell analysis pipelines for robust annotation and discovery
abstract: Accurate cell-type annotation in single-cell RNA sequencing is sensitive to upstream parameters often selected heuristically. We introduce scBOA, a two-stage framework that uses Bayesian optimization to select workflow parameters against a prespecified objective and reruns the selected configuration for reference-assisted analysis. Its configurable objectives combine annotation purity, marker concordance and transcriptomic cohesion, enabling fine-grained or conservative solutions. Optional extensions support low-confidence-cell refinement and multi-sample integration. Across simulations and fluorescence-activated cell sorting datasets of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells, pancreas and adult heart, we compare Gaussian-process scBOA with 14 alternative parameter-selection and clustering strategies. We show that performance depends on the objective, workflow, reference hierarchy and vocabulary, consensus-label construction and partition granularity. We find that scBOA is not uniformly superior, but shows strong aggregate performance when annotation targets align with biological structure. We apply a mouse Huntington’s disease dataset as an exploratory stress test of integration and reference mapping. Overall, we demonstrate that scBOA provides reproducible, objective-driven workflow optimization for reference-assisted single-cell analysis.

title: CPRISP: an interpretable deep learning framework predicting circRNA-RBP interactions and guiding therapeutic discovery in neurodegeneration
abstract: Circular RNAs regulate gene expression through interactions with ribonucleic acid binding proteins, but their binding sites remain difficult to predict across proteins and cellular contexts. Existing methods often focus on transcript features while making limited use of protein-specific information and structural context. Here, we show that an integrated deep learning framework combining circular transcript sequence composition, physicochemical properties, secondary structure, pretrained representations and protein features improves interaction-site prediction across 37 benchmark datasets and generalizes across cell lines; model interpretation recovers conserved single-stranded sequence patterns, while analyses of proteins linked to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis identify recurrent pathways involving nucleocytoplasmic transport, lysosomal signaling and guanosine triphosphatase activity and prioritize compounds for experimental follow-up, supporting accurate and interpretable mapping of circular ribonucleic acid protein interactions without implying therapeutic efficacy.

title: Sequence Display generates large-scale sequence–activity datasets for reprogramming SlugCas9 toward difficult-to-access PAMs
abstract: Protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) requirements constrain the targeting scope of CRISPR-Cas9 systems and limit genome editing applications that require precise nuclease positioning. Although broad-PAM and near-PAMless Cas9 variants have expanded the editable genome, robust targeting across certain PAM families remains difficult, particularly at NNAN PAMs. Here, we apply Sequence Display to generate multiplexed, large-scale sequence–activity datasets for Staphylococcus lugdunensis Cas9 (SlugCas9) across the NNAN PAM family, including NNAA, NNAT, NNAC and NNAG. These datasets quantitatively resolve how individual and combinatorial mutations reshape nuclease activity across distinct PAM contexts. By integrating Sequence Display-derived datasets with protein language models, we construct fine-grained activity landscapes and identify SlugCas9 variants with enhanced and broadened activity across NNAN PAMs. The resulting variants reprogram PAM recognition beyond the native G-compatible landscape of SlugCas9 and enable improved base editing at selected endogenous NNAN-constrained sites in cultured mammalian cells, including disease-relevant sites in APOC3 and PCSK9 . Together, our results establish a strategy for reprogramming PAM preference in compact Cas9 nucleases and highlight Sequence Display as a general platform for evolving genome editors toward specific and difficult-to-access PAM spaces.

title: IDPForge: deep learning of proteins with global and local regions of disorder
abstract: Although machine learning has transformed protein structure prediction of folded protein ground states with remarkable accuracy, intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs) are defined by diverse and dynamical structural ensembles that are predicted with low confidence by algorithms such as AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold. We present a machine learning method, IDPForge ( I ntrinsically D isordered P rotein, FO lded and disordered R egion GE nerator), that exploits a transformer protein language diffusion model to create all-atom IDP ensembles and IDR ensembles that maintains the folded domains. IDPForge does not require sequence-specific training, back transformations from coarse-grained representations, nor ensemble reweighting. The created IDP/IDR conformational ensembles show good agreement with both NMR and SAXS solution experimental data, and options for biasing with experimental restraints are available if desired. IDPForge with these diverse capabilities facilitates integrative and structural studies for proteins that contain intrinsic disorder, and is available as an open source resource for general use.

title: Neanderthal introgressed ancestry reveals human genomic regions enriched with recessive deleterious mutations
abstract: Negative selection on deleterious mutations plays a key role in shaping human genetic variation, yet the dominance effects of these mutations remain poorly understood because existing statistical methods often cannot distinguish dominance effects from the overall selective effects. In this work, we take a fundamentally different approach by leveraging the distribution of Neanderthal ancestry across the human genome. Simulations show that recessive deleterious mutations can increase archaic introgressed ancestry through heterosis in the absence of positive selection, in contrast to the depletion expected under additive effects. We use this signal to develop DominL , a machine learning classifier trained on simulations of human demography with Neanderthal introgression to identify megabase-scale genomic windows enriched with recessive mutations. DominL demonstrates robust accuracy, with particularly high power in exon-dense regions. Applied to 7 non-African populations from the 1000 Genomes Project, DominL identifies approximately 3-9% of the genome as enriched for recessive mutations, with most high-confidence regions shared across populations. Predicted regions show patterns consistent with expected signatures from recessive mutations, including weakened background selection, depletion of runs of homozygosity, and enrichment of non-additive trait-associated variants. These regions also contain genes associated with metabolic and immune-related functions.

title: AI-driven discovery and engineering of human-derived protein scaffolds for mRNA delivery
abstract: Safe and effective gene delivery remains a central challenge for therapeutic applications. While non-viral and viral vectors have enabled substantial progress, their reliance on non-human components often triggers immune responses, limiting their use in chronic treatments. Here, we develop DeepDelivery, an artificial intelligence-driven platform to identify human proteins with scaffold potential for mRNA delivery. Proteome-scale screening nominated 512 candidates, and experimental validation show that 12 of 15 selected human proteins functioned as scaffold components that facilitated particle formation and mRNA delivery within a modular engineering framework. Notably, several tripartite motif (TRIM) family proteins, typically linked to antiviral responses, exhibit strong assembly and delivery activity. Model interpretability and perturbation analyses identify TRIM domain features that influenced prediction scores and guide TRIM25-specific domain engineering to improve delivery. Together, these results establish a framework for mining the human proteome for scaffold components of programmable mRNA delivery systems and for further exploring the design space of human-derived delivery architectures.

title: Fairness in infectious disease modeling
abstract: The concept of fairness has been extensively examined within the domains of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence more broadly. It remains, however, largely underexplored in the field of Computational Epidemiology. Considering the substantial influence that epidemic models exert on public health policy, particularly in the context of outbreak preparedness and response, this shortcoming is of great relevance. Here, we propose a mathematical framework, grounded in core principles from Social Epidemiology, for evaluating the fairness of computational epidemic models. We begin by applying our framework to a range of epidemic modeling approaches and simulation scenarios, such as the initial spread of COVID-19 in London, New York, and Santiago de Chile, as well as the 2016 Zika virus outbreak in Colombia, demonstrating its consistent capacity to assess model fairness across diverse disease dynamics. Subsequently, we illustrate how our definition of fairness can be incorporated into the design of immunization strategies as a way to enhance health equity while simultaneously improving the overall effectiveness of such interventions. Overall, our results offer a new systematic methodology for quantifying fairness in computational epidemiology.
